SiYuan Electron renderer spawns shell/LOLBin (CVE-2026-50551 AV-cell XSS-to-RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts the terminal stage of CVE-2026-50551/CVE-2026-54158: a stored XSS in the attribute-view cell renderer (genAVValueHTML) fires when a victim opens the block-attribute panel, and because the Electron desktop build runs nodeIntegration:true it chains to host RCE via require('child_process').exec(). SiYuan is a note-taking app and has no legitimate reason to spawn cmd/powershell/calc, so any shell or LOLBin child of SiYuan.exe is high-fidelity for exploitation. Rationale: Anchored on the exact RCE primitive the advisory and corroborating sources confirm — require('child_process').exec('calc') from the SiYuan Electron renderer (nodeIntegration:true). SiYuan.exe parenting a shell/calc/LOLBin has effectively no benign baseline, making this alert-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-56mp-4f3v-fgj2 • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/security/advisories/GHSA-4663-4mpg-879v • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-44670/ • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-54158
ATT&CKT1203 T1059.007 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SiYuan plugin or user-invoked feature that legitimately shells out (rare; some community plugins call external tools)
  • Developer running SiYuan from source/Electron dev build spawning node/cmd during debugging
  • EDR/AV emulation or sandbox detonation of a SiYuan build inflating the child-process count
  • Update/installer routine launched from within the app spawning cmd.exe or bitsadmin
  • Screen-capture or 'open in terminal' integrations a power user configured
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--updater","siyuan-updater") and FileName =~ "cmd.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the child ProcessCommandLine and InitiatingProcessCommandLine — a benign launch has a plausible target (opening a URL/file); an exploit shows exec('calc'), whoami, curl/certutil download, or an encoded payload. Confirm the SiYuan version on the host (<3.7.0 is vulnerable). 2) Contain: Isolate the endpoint, kill the SiYuan.exe process tree, and quarantine the workspace's data/storage/av/*.json files as they hold the stored payload. 3) Hunt: Identify the tainted avID and search all peers that sync the same workspace for the same file and for SiYuan.exe→shell events; rotate the sync credentials (SiYuan Cloud / S3 / WebDAV) used to plant it and force-upgrade all clients to 3.7.0.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "SiYuan.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","calc.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","bash.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\SiYuan.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\regsvr32.exe","\\calc.exe","\\curl.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\bash.exe")
| where not(Account endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ProcessId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Non-SiYuan process writes attribute-view JSON under data/storage/av (CVE-2026-50551 payload plant/sync) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the persistence/propagation stage of CVE-2026-50551/CVE-2026-54158: the malicious attribute-view cell persists byte-for-byte in data/storage/av/<avID>.json because the kernel never HTML-escapes on write, then rides normal workspace sync to every peer. This surfaces AV JSON files being written by a process OTHER than SiYuan.exe (e.g. a sync daemon dropping the tainted file on a peer, or hand-planting), which is where the payload enters or arrives on a host. Rationale: Uses the advisory's exact backing-store path (data/storage/av/<avID>.json) and the fact that the kernel writes it unescaped and it rides sync. Filtering to writers other than SiYuan.exe isolates payload plant/arrival (sync daemons, editors) rather than the app's own routine saves — a genuine article-specific pivot, kept at hunting tier since file telemetry can't see the payload content. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-56mp-4f3v-fgj2 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-44670/
ATT&CKT1080 T1546 T1608.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate cloud-sync clients (Dropbox.exe, syncthing.exe, rclone.exe, OneDrive) syncing benign attribute-view edits between the user's own devices
  • Backup software (Veeam, restic, robocopy) copying the workspace including av/*.json
  • A user editing/restoring a workspace with a text editor or file manager
  • SiYuan running under a renamed or portable executable so the process name isn't literally SiYuan.exe
  • Antivirus or indexer touching/rewriting the file during a scan
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("OneDrive.exe","Dropbox.exe","googledrivesync.exe","FileCoAuth.exe") and InitiatingProcessFileName !endswith "backup.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: Note the writing process — a sync daemon (syncthing/rclone/Dropbox) or non-SiYuan editor on multiple hosts writing the same avID is the propagation signal. Manually inspect the flagged data/storage/av/<avID>.json for breakout markers (</textarea>, \"><img, onerror=, require('child_process')). 2) Contain: Quarantine the offending JSON on every host it landed on and pause the workspace sync channel so the payload stops spreading; block opening the block-attribute panel until clients are patched. 3) Hunt: Pivot on the avID across all synced peers, correlate to any SiYuan.exe→shell executions (UC1), and review sync-service/identity logs for the account/IP that first wrote the tainted cell; upgrade all clients to SiYuan 3.7.0.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has @"\data\storage\av\" and FileName endswith ".json"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !~ "SiYuan.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FileCount = dcount(FileName), Files = make_set(FileName, 20), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\data\storage\av\" and TargetFileName endswith ".json"
| where not(ActingProcessName has "SiYuan.exe")
| summarize FileCount = dcount(TargetFileName), Files = make_set(TargetFileName, 20), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
| order by LastSeen desc

File Browser hook-auth pre-auth RCE: filebrowser spawns shell/recon commands (CVE-2026-54088) AIExploitation High
Hunts the File Browser server binary (`filebrowser`) spawning a shell or OS discovery/tooling child process. Under CVE-2026-54088 an unauthenticated attacker injects shell metacharacters into the login username/password, which `os.Expand` substitutes unsanitised into the admin's hook-auth command, causing the `filebrowser` process to execute attacker OS commands. A file server should essentially never spawn `id`/`whoami`/`curl`/`wget`, so any such child is high-fidelity. Rationale: Uses the concrete vulnerable binary name `filebrowser` (parent) plus the article's PoC injection primitive (shell metacharacters `;`/`$(`/backtick and `id`/`whoami` running under the hook command). A file-server process spawning recon/OS tooling is near-zero in benign operation. Cross-checked against filebrowser.org auth docs and auth/hook.go on GitHub. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m93h-4hw7-5qcm • https://filebrowser.org/authentication.html • https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/blob/master/auth/hook.go
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1033 T1087.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin legitimately configured a hook-auth command that shells out to an external auth backend using curl/wget (e.g. validating against an LDAP/OIDC gateway)
  • Custom container entrypoint or healthcheck wrapper also named 'filebrowser' spawning /bin/sh for readiness probes
  • Ops running the filebrowser CLI (`filebrowser config`, `filebrowser users`) interactively from a shell where the parent/child order is inverted
  • Backup/maintenance scripts invoked by a filebrowser-named systemd unit that call uname/hostname
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash") and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"^\s*test\s" and not (ProcessCommandLine matches regex @";|\|\||&&|\$\(|\x60"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the alert — confirm InitiatingProcessFileName=='filebrowser' and inspect the child ProcessCommandLine for injected recon (id/whoami/cat /etc/passwd) or separators; correlate to the host's web/reverse-proxy logs for a POST to /api/login in the same second. 2) Contain: isolate the host, stop the filebrowser container/service, and disable hook authentication (set auth.method back to json/proxy) or patch to filebrowser v2 > 2.63.5. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for follow-on egress/reverse shells (UC2), new files under the served directory (webshell/backdoor), new cron entries or SSH authorized_keys, and any outbound connection from the filebrowser process subtree.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "filebrowser"
| where (FileName in~ ("id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","netcat","socat","python","python3","perl","ruby","php"))
    or (FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ash","zsh","ksh")
        and (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","whoami","uname","/dev/tcp/")
             or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @";|\|\||&&|\$\(|\x60"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "filebrowser" or ParentProcessName has "filebrowser"
| where (TargetProcessName has_any ("/id","/whoami","/uname","/hostname","/curl","/wget","/nc","/ncat","/socat","/python","/perl","/ruby","/php"))
    or (TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/ash","/zsh","/ksh")
        and (TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","whoami","uname","/dev/tcp/")
             or TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @";|\|\||&&|\$\(|\x60"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File Browser hook-auth RCE follow-on: reverse shell / egress tooling under filebrowser (CVE-2026-54088) AICommand & Control High
Hunts the File Browser process subtree spawning a reverse shell or ingress/download tool after successful command injection. Distinct from the discovery UC: this targets the C2 stage where the injected command establishes an interactive shell (`bash -i`, `/dev/tcp/`, `nc -e`, `socat`, `mkfifo`) or pulls a second-stage payload (`curl`/`wget` piped to a shell) from the `filebrowser` process. Rationale: Pairs the concrete vulnerable parent binary `filebrowser` with high-specificity reverse-shell/ingress signatures (`/dev/tcp/`, `bash -i`, `nc -e`, `socat`, `curl|wget` piped to shell) from the RCE class described in the advisory. These command-line strings are near-zero-FP and map the exploit to its C2/second-stage phase. Corroborated via filebrowser.org auth docs and the GHSA advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m93h-4hw7-5qcm • https://filebrowser.org/authentication.html • https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/blob/master/auth/hook.go
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1105 T1571
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit hook-auth command that uses curl/wget to POST credentials to an external authentication API
  • filebrowser sidecar/init script that pulls config or TLS certs via curl/wget at startup
  • Admin debugging the container with `docker exec` where the shell's parent resolves to filebrowser
  • Monitoring agent invoking python from within the filebrowser service context for metrics
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("https://auth.","/certs/","/token") and ProcessCommandLine !has "/dev/tcp/" and ProcessCommandLine !has "| sh" and ProcessCommandLine !has "|sh")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the child ProcessCommandLine and resolve the destination host/port (grep for the IP after /dev/tcp/ or the nc/socat/curl target); check DeviceNetworkEvents on the same host for a matching outbound public connection in the same window. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the filebrowser process/container, block the observed C2 IP/domain at the egress firewall, and rotate any credentials/secrets readable by the filebrowser service account. 3) Hunt: search for downloaded second-stage files, persistence (cron, systemd units, authorized_keys), lateral SSH from this host, and repeat the UC1 discovery query to scope earlier recon.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "filebrowser"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ash","zsh","ksh","nc","ncat","netcat","socat","curl","wget","python","python3","perl")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","bash -i","sh -i","mkfifo","socat","import socket","import pty","curl ","wget ")
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\bnc(\.traditional)?\b.*\s-[ec]\b"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "filebrowser" or ParentProcessName has "filebrowser"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/ash","/zsh","/ksh","/nc","/ncat","/socat","/curl","/wget","/python","/perl")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","bash -i","sh -i","mkfifo","socat","import socket","import pty","curl ","wget ")
    or TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\bnc(\.traditional)?\b.*\s-[ec]\b"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FileBrowser proxy-auth bypass: direct-to-app /api/login from non-proxy source IP (CVE-2026-54089) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the CVE-2026-54089 header-forgery entry point. In auth.method=proxy deployments the reverse proxy (Authelia/Authentik/OAuth2-Proxy/Caddy forward_auth) must be the ONLY client the FileBrowser app ever sees; any second source IP POSTing /api/login reached the app directly and can forge X-Remote-User to bypass SSO. Surfaces every distinct client IP hitting the login endpoint so a non-proxy attacker stands out. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete auth.method=proxy design flaw plus the exact login endpoint (POST /api/login) and process name (filebrowser). The 'single legitimate client IP' invariant of proxy-auth makes distinct-client-count a high-signal, low-invention heuristic for the direct-to-app forgery path. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm • https://app.opencve.io/cve/?vendor=filebrowser • https://filebrowserquantum.com/en/docs/configuration/authentication/proxy/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Highly-available deployments running two or more reverse-proxy front-ends (multiple legitimate proxy IPs)
  • Health-check/monitoring probes (Docker healthcheck, Prometheus blackbox, load-balancer probe) hitting /api/login directly
  • Admin debugging the container by curling the published port from a workstation
  • Blue-team/vuln-scanner (Nessus, Nuclei) authenticated scan of the app port
  • IPv6/NAT churn where the proxy egresses from a rotating address pool
Suppression filter
| where DistinctClients > 1   // after enumerating ClientIPs, drop the known proxy set: e.g. | mv-expand ClientIPs | where ClientIPs !in ('<enumerate your proxy egress IPs from the make_set output>')
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the FileBrowser instance runs auth.method=proxy and identify the sanctioned reverse-proxy egress IP(s); any client IP on /api/login that is not that proxy is the attacker. 2) Contain: firewall the app port so it only accepts the proxy (bind 127.0.0.1 or restrict security group), and rotate the FileBrowser JWT signing key to invalidate any minted admin tokens. 3) Hunt: from the offending source IP, pull all subsequent /api/settings, /api/users and /api/resources requests, and review the FileBrowser user DB for accounts created around that time (auto-creation primitive) — disable any not provisioned by an admin.
// Network-layer view: inbound connections landing directly on the FileBrowser process from a public/non-proxy source (proxy-auth is meant to front all traffic).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "filebrowser"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize Connections = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Ports = make_set(LocalPort, 5) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName
| sort by Connections desc
// In proxy-auth mode the app should only ever see the reverse-proxy IP; >1 distinct client on /api/login = direct-to-app bypass path.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where HttpMethod == "POST"
| where Url has "/api/login"
| summarize LoginEvents = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), ClientIPs = make_set(SrcIpAddr, 20) by DstHostname
| extend DistinctClients = array_length(ClientIPs)
| where DistinctClients > 1   // 1 expected = the reverse proxy; more = someone reached the app directly
| sort by DistinctClients desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| stats dc(src) as distinct_clients values(src) as client_ips sum(login_events) as login_events min(firstTime) as firstTime max(lastTime) as lastTime by dest site
| where distinct_clients > 1
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - distinct_clients
| tstats summariesonly=false count as login_events min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where (Web.http_method="POST" AND Web.url="*/api/login*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.site
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| where distinct_clients > 1
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - distinct_clients
FileBrowser forged-admin-JWT use: /api/login immediately followed by admin-only /api/settings or /api/users AIExploitation High
Detects the CVE-2026-54089 privilege-escalation moment: after forging X-Remote-User to mint a valid admin JWT, the attacker reads full server config and enumerates every account. Correlates a POST /api/login with a successful GET to admin-only /api/settings or /api/users from the same client within a 2-minute window — the exact exploit walk from the advisory's attack-flow diagram. Rationale: Chains the two article-named endpoints from the exploit flow (POST /api/login -> GET /api/settings + /api/users) with the 200-status admin gate. A fresh login followed within seconds by successful admin-config and full-user enumeration is the signature of a header-minted admin JWT, not normal usage. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm • https://filebrowserquantum.com/en/docs/configuration/authentication/proxy/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1078.001
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine FileBrowser administrator logging in and immediately opening the Settings/Users admin panels (both /api/settings and /api/users fire on the admin UI load)
  • Automation/backup tooling using a real admin service account that polls /api/settings after re-auth
  • Config-management job that logs in and reads settings to reconcile state
  • Post-upgrade smoke test that logs in and verifies the admin API responds 200
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ('<your reverse-proxy egress IPs>') // legitimate admin access arrives via the proxy; direct client IPs are the true positives
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether the correlated SrcIpAddr is the sanctioned reverse-proxy IP; if it is not, the admin JWT was almost certainly forged (no password/bcrypt event backs it). Pull the raw login request headers if the proxy/WAF captured them and look for a client-supplied X-Remote-User. 2) Contain: rotate the FileBrowser JWT signing secret to revoke all live tokens and restrict the app port to the proxy only. 3) Hunt: enumerate every /api/resources and download request from that client/token, and audit the user table for accounts created via the auto-provisioning primitive; remove any rogue accounts and force re-auth for all users.
let Window = 2m;
let Logins = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
    | where HttpMethod == "POST" and Url has "/api/login"
    | project LoginTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where HttpMethod == "GET"
| where Url has_any ("/api/settings", "/api/users")
| where HttpStatusCode == 200   // admin-only endpoints returning 200 = token carried admin perms
| join kind=inner Logins on SrcIpAddr, $left.DstHostname == $right.DstHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (LoginTime .. LoginTime + Window)

FileBrowser post-takeover enumeration & file collection burst from single client (CVE-2026-54089) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the discovery/collection stage after CVE-2026-54089 admin takeover: one client reads server config (/api/settings), enumerates all accounts (/api/users), and then browses a large number of distinct file scopes (/api/resources) to impersonate users and harvest their files. Thresholds on breadth of resource paths combined with admin-endpoint access from a single source. Rationale: Maps the advisory's discovery/collection claims ('read full server config', 'enumerate every user', 'impersonate users, access their files') onto the three concrete endpoints /api/settings, /api/users and /api/resources. Requiring admin-config + user-enumeration + wide resource-path fan-out from one client filters normal per-user browsing. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm
ATT&CKT1087 T1005
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate administrator doing bulk file management across many users' scopes in one session (also touches /api/settings and /api/users)
  • Backup/sync agent walking all shares via /api/resources under a real admin token
  • Migration or indexing tooling crawling every path after an upgrade
  • The reverse-proxy IP aggregating many users' traffic into one apparent client (all users egress as the proxy IP) — must be excluded or the proxy will trip the threshold
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ('<your reverse-proxy egress IPs>')  // exclude the proxy which fronts all legitimate users; and optionally exclude known admin/backup service source IPs
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SrcIpAddr is not the reverse proxy; a non-proxy client that read config, listed all users, and crawled 20+ resource scopes is exfiltration-grade behaviour. Correlate back to a preceding /api/login (UC2) to confirm the forged-token origin. 2) Contain: revoke tokens by rotating the JWT signing key, lock the app port to the proxy, and snapshot access logs for IR. 3) Hunt: identify which users' file scopes were accessed and what was downloaded (response sizes on /api/resources GETs), notify data owners, and scan for rogue auto-created accounts left for persistence.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where Url has_any ("/api/settings", "/api/users", "/api/resources")
| summarize
    SettingsHits = countif(Url has "/api/settings"),
    UsersHits    = countif(Url has "/api/users"),
    DistinctResourcePaths = dcountif(Url, Url has "/api/resources"),
    FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname
| where SettingsHits > 0 and UsersHits > 0 and DistinctResourcePaths > 20   // 20 = broad multi-scope browsing in one window; benign single users don't read settings+users+dozens of scopes
| sort by DistinctResourcePaths desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Exposure hunt: hosts running a vulnerable SiYuan kernel listening on port 6806 · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Web browser process connecting to SiYuan kernel admin API on 127.0.0.1:6806
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation

Web browser process connecting to SiYuan kernel admin API on 127.0.0.1:6806 AIDelivery Medium
Hunts a real Chrome/Chromium browser process opening a loopback connection to the SiYuan Note kernel HTTP server (127.0.0.1:6806). Because SiYuan's own Electron UI runs as SiYuan.exe, a connection to 6806 originating from chrome.exe/msedge.exe/brave.exe indicates a browser extension (potentially a compromised one) abusing the blanket chrome-extension:// origin allowlist (CVE-2026-54069) to make unauthenticated RoleAdministrator API calls. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete exploit primitive: the SiYuan kernel listens on 127.0.0.1:6806 and the exploit path is a browser extension (running inside chrome.exe/msedge.exe, not SiYuan.exe) opening a loopback connection to that port. Filtering initiating process to real browsers excludes the legitimate SiYuan.exe Electron UI. Port 6806 and the loopback address are corroborated by cve.threatint.eu and DeepWiki SiYuan deployment docs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hvr9-72v2-fff3 • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-54069 • https://deepwiki.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/6-building-and-deployment
ATT&CKT1176 T1005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The official SiYuan Web Clipper browser extension legitimately POSTing captured content to 127.0.0.1:6806
  • User opening the SiYuan kernel UI directly in a Chrome tab via http://127.0.0.1:6806 (browser-access mode)
  • Developer testing the SiYuan API from browser DevTools or a self-authored extension
  • An unrelated local application coincidentally bound to TCP 6806 that a browser also contacts
  • EDR agents that intermittently emit loopback ConnectionAttempt without a matching ConnectionSuccess
Response runbook
1) Triage: On the flagged host, confirm SiYuan version (vuln <= 3.6.5) and enumerate installed browser extensions for the offending browser profile; determine whether the SiYuan Web Clipper is installed (benign) or an unexpected/recently-updated extension is the source. 2) Contain: If an unknown/compromised extension is implicated, remove it, force-close the browser, and set a non-empty AccessAuthCode in SiYuan; upgrade SiYuan to >= 3.7.0. 3) Hunt: Pivot on the same host for follow-on impact — new/modified notes containing injected <img onerror=...> or <script> payloads (stored XSS), SiYuan config changes, and any subsequent outbound connection from SiYuan.exe or the browser to an external host that could be document-exfil / cookie theft.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 6806
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe","chromium.exe","chrome_proxy.exe")
| summarize ConnCount=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by LastSeen desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 6806
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe","chromium.exe","chrome_proxy.exe")
| summarize ConnCount=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by LastSeen desc
title: Web Browser Connecting to SiYuan Kernel Admin API on Loopback 6806
id: 6f2a1c94-3d1e-4b8a-9c77-2e5f0a9d1b44
description: Detects a Chrome/Chromium browser process connecting to the SiYuan Note kernel HTTP server on 127.0.0.1:6806, indicating a browser extension abusing the blanket chrome-extension origin allowlist (CVE-2026-54069).
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hvr9-72v2-fff3
  - https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-54069
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/10
tags:
  - attack.t1176
  - attack.t1005
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Initiated: 'true'
    DestinationPort: 6806
    DestinationIp:
      - '127.0.0.1'
      - '::1'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
      - '\brave.exe'
      - '\opera.exe'
      - '\vivaldi.exe'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationPort:6806 (@DestinationIp:127.0.0.1 OR @DestinationIp:"::1") @Image:(*\chrome.exe OR *\Chrome.exe OR *\msedge.exe OR *\MsEdge.exe OR *\brave.exe OR *\Brave.exe OR *\opera.exe OR *\vivaldi.exe OR *\chromium.exe)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemotePort=6806 RemoteAddressIP4=/^127\.0\.0\.1$/ ContextImageFileName=/\\(chrome|msedge|brave|opera|vivaldi|chromium)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=6806 (All_Traffic.dest="127.0.0.1" OR All_Traffic.dest="::1") (All_Traffic.process_name="chrome.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="msedge.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="brave.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="opera.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="vivaldi.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="chromium.exe") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.process_name All_Traffic.user | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=6806 (All_Traffic.dest="127.0.0.1" OR All_Traffic.dest="::1") (All_Traffic.process_name="chrome.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="msedge.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="brave.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="opera.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="vivaldi.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="chromium.exe") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.process_name All_Traffic.user | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Exposure hunt: hosts running a vulnerable SiYuan kernel listening on port 6806 AIReconnaissance High
Asset-exposure hunt that surfaces every endpoint running the SiYuan Note kernel bound to port 6806, capturing the binary's product version so IT/SOC can identify installs at or below the vulnerable v3.6.5 for CVE-2026-54069. This is the pre-emptive companion to the exploit-traffic detection: any listed host with an empty AccessAuthCode is trivially exploitable by any installed browser extension. Rationale: Grounded in the article's concrete facts: the SiYuan kernel binds 127.0.0.1:6806 and versions <= v3.6.5 (commit 96dfe0bea474) are vulnerable, fixed in 3.7.0. The listener-on-6806 pivot plus InitiatingProcessVersionInfoProductVersion identifies both the exposed service and its patch level in one pass; the Sentinel variant leans on the TVM CVE catalog for CVE-2026-54069. Port and version corroborated by cve.threatint.eu and DeepWiki deployment docs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hvr9-72v2-fff3 • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-54069 • https://deepwiki.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/6-building-and-deployment
ATT&CKT1190 T1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts already upgraded to SiYuan >= 3.7.0 still listening on 6806 (patched, not vulnerable — verify version column)
  • A non-SiYuan local service that happens to bind port 6806
  • SiYuan running in Docker/self-hosted mode where a non-empty AccessAuthCode is enforced (reduced risk)
  • TVM catalog lag where CVE-2026-54069 is not yet mapped, causing the Sentinel variant to under-report until inventory sync
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessVersionInfoProductVersion !in ("3.7.0","3.7.1") and toint(coalesce(extract(@"^(\d+)", 1, InitiatingProcessVersionInfoProductVersion), "0")) <= 3
Response runbook
1) Triage: For each surfaced host, read the SiYuan product version — flag any <= 3.6.5 as immediately exploitable and confirm whether AccessAuthCode is empty (desktop default). 2) Contain: Push upgrade to SiYuan >= 3.7.0 and/or instruct users to set a non-empty AccessAuthCode; where feasible, restrict the 6806 listener and review installed browser extensions on the same host. 3) Hunt: For every vulnerable host, run the companion detection (browser process → 127.0.0.1:6806) over the prior 30 days to determine whether the exposed API was actually contacted by a browser extension, and inspect notes for injected stored-XSS payloads.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ListeningConnectionCreated"
| where LocalPort == 6806
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessVersionInfoProductVersion
| order by LastSeen desc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-54069" or (SoftwareName has "siyuan")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by TimeGenerated desc
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\siyuan\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, FileVersion], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` values(Processes.process_version) as version min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="siyuan.exe" by Processes.dest Processes.process_name Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false values(Processes.process_version) as version min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="siyuan.exe" by Processes.dest Processes.process_name Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).

Authorizer /authorize implicit-flow token leak via unvalidated redirect_uri (CVE-2026-54072) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP requests to the Authorizer /authorize endpoint using the implicit flow (response_type=token or id_token) that carry a redirect_uri, and surfaces the redirect_uri host for allowlist comparison. The vulnerable handler appends access_token/id_token/refresh_token and 302-redirects to any attacker-supplied URL, so an off-origin redirect_uri on the implicit flow is the exploitation signal. Rationale: Uses the article's exact vulnerable endpoint (/authorize), the implicit-flow trigger (response_type=token / id_token) and the redirect_uri parameter that lacks IsValidOrigin() validation; projects the decoded redirect_uri host so an analyst can compare it against the deployment's AllowedOrigins. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h29v-hj44-q8cv • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x3f4-v83f-7wp2
ATT&CKT1190 T1528
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimately registered SPA client using the implicit flow with a redirect_uri that IS in AllowedOrigins
  • Security scanners / DAST tools (Burp, ZAP) probing /authorize during authorized pentests
  • Internal QA/staging traffic pointing redirect_uri at test hostnames
  • Legacy first-party app still on implicit flow before migration to auth-code+PKCE
Suppression filter
| where redirect_host !in~ ("your-authorizer-host.example.com")   // analyst: replace with AllowedOrigins hostnames
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract redirect_host from the hit and compare against the Authorizer AllowedOrigins config; an off-origin/attacker domain confirms exploitation. Check scStatus for 302 and the source IP/user-agent. 2) Contain: patch Authorizer to a build >= 0.0.0-20260409051328-bd3f5baf6d3d (adds IsValidOrigin on /authorize); if patching is delayed, block implicit-flow response_types at the WAF and force affected users to reset sessions/rotate refresh tokens. 3) Hunt: pivot on the redirect_host and any recon of /graphql {meta{client_id}} from the same IP, and review /userinfo access with tokens shortly after the redirect to spot token replay.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/authorize"
| where Url has "response_type=token" or Url has "response_type=id_token"
| where Url has "redirect_uri="
| extend redirect_uri = url_decode(extract(@"redirect_uri=([^&]+)", 1, Url))
| extend redirect_host = tolower(extract(@"^https?://([^/]+)", 1, redirect_uri))
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, redirect_host, redirect_uri, Url, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Unauthenticated GraphQL client_id disclosure recon on Authorizer (CVE-2026-54072 precursor) AIReconnaissance Low
Hunts unauthenticated GraphQL requests that pull the public client_id via the {meta{client_id}} query — the recon step the advisory shows an attacker running before crafting the malicious /authorize link. Catches the GET-form query in URL telemetry; POST-body variants need WAF body logging. Rationale: Uses the advisory's exact recon query path (/graphql) and the {meta{client_id}} field names an attacker fetches with no auth; low confidence because the reproduce uses a POST body (not always in URL logs) and GraphQL client_id fetch can be benign SPA bootstrap traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h29v-hj44-q8cv • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x3f4-v83f-7wp2
ATT&CKT1595 T1592
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate first-party SPA fetching its own client_id at page load (this endpoint is public by design)
  • Uptime/synthetic monitors hitting /graphql meta query
  • Internal integration tests enumerating meta fields
  • Search-engine or asset-discovery crawlers indexing the GraphQL endpoint
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("10.0.0.0")   // analyst: exclude known first-party SPA / monitoring egress IPs
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is external and not a known SPA origin or monitor; note the user-agent (scripted clients like python/curl are higher signal). 2) Contain: no direct block needed (endpoint is public) but flag the IP and watch for a follow-on /authorize implicit-flow request from any victim within the session window. 3) Hunt: correlate the recon IP against later /authorize?response_type=token requests carrying off-origin redirect_uri (UC1) and any /userinfo Bearer replay to build the full chain.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/graphql"
| where Url has "meta" and Url has "client_id"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, Url, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SiYuan Electron renderer (nodeIntegration) spawning shell/LOLBin child — XSS-to-RCE AIExploitation High
Hunts the RCE stage of CVE-2026-54067 (and the sibling SiYuan XSS-to-RCE bugs): a stored snippet/caption/README breaks out of its HTML context and, because the renderer runs with nodeIntegration:true, calls require('child_process') to spawn a command interpreter. A Markdown note app should essentially never parent cmd.exe/powershell.exe, so this parent->child pair is high-fidelity across the whole SiYuan RCE bug class. Rationale: Anchored on InitiatingProcessFileName=siyuan.exe (the Electron main/renderer binary confirmed in the advisory as running nodeIntegration:true/contextIsolation:false) parenting a command interpreter — the observable end state of require('child_process').execSync from injected JS. Node's execSync on Windows spawns cmd.exe, making cmd.exe the highest-value child. Robust across all SiYuan XSS-to-RCE variants. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/security/advisories/GHSA-phhp-9rm9-6gr2 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-44670/ • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-54067
ATT&CKT1203 T1059.003 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SiYuan document export to PDF/Word invoking a bundled pandoc/wkhtmltopdf helper (verify child binary is the export helper, not a shell)
  • User-configured 'open with' / external-command plugins in SiYuan that legitimately shell out
  • A power-user snippet the owner wrote themselves that intentionally calls a benign command (confirm with the user)
  • SiYuan auto-update or crash-reporter helper launched via cmd.exe wrapper
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has_any ("pandoc", "wkhtmltopdf", "--export", "SiYuan-Kernel"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the child ProcessCommandLine and SHA256 — a benign export helper looks nothing like a shell one-liner. Check whether the same user recently edited a CSS/JS snippet or synced a workspace. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the child process tree, and revoke/rotate any SiYuan Cloud / S3 / WebDAV sync credentials for that workspace so the poisoned snippet can't re-propagate. 3) HUNT: Retrieve data/snippets/conf.json from every peer that syncs the same workspace and grep for '</style>' or 'onerror='; upgrade all SiYuan clients to >=3.7.0; sweep other hosts for siyuan.exe parenting interpreters over the last 30 days.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "siyuan.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","calc.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\siyuan.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\regsvr32.exe","\\curl.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\calc.exe")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Non-SiYuan process writing synced snippet store data\snippets\conf.json AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the plant/delivery stage of CVE-2026-54067: the malicious CSS snippet is stored in the workspace file data/snippets/conf.json, which syncs to every peer. When a process OTHER than the SiYuan kernel writes that file — e.g. a Dropbox/Syncthing/Google Drive sync client, a text editor, or a shared-drive process — it indicates the snippet store was tampered with out-of-band, exactly the 'workspace-write compromise via shared filesystem' vector the advisory calls out. Rationale: Uses the exact storage path from the advisory (data/snippets/conf.json, referenced at kernel/model/repository.go:1748,1798) and excludes the legitimate writer (the SiYuan kernel). A write by a sync client or editor is the out-of-band tamper path the advisory enumerates (Dropbox/Syncthing/network share/git). Cross-checked against: • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-54067 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-44670/
ATT&CKT1080 T1195
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Dropbox.exe / SyncthingTray.exe / googledrivefs.exe legitimately syncing a workspace whose owner edited snippets on another device (benign but the exact tamper vector — inspect the resulting content)
  • A backup agent (Veeam, Duplicati, Acronis) reading/rewriting the workspace folder
  • User editing conf.json directly in VS Code / Notepad++ during troubleshooting
  • Git client (git.exe) pulling a workspace tracked in version control
  • Antivirus/EDR quarantine-and-restore touching the file
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","duplicati.exe","backup.exe") and InitiatingProcessFileName !endswith "git.exe"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Open the written data/snippets/conf.json and grep for '</style>', 'onerror=', '<img', or 'child_process' — a benign sync writes normal CSS/JS. Note the writing process and account. 2) CONTAIN: If payload strings are present, quarantine the workspace, block sync (pause Dropbox/Syncthing, revoke WebDAV/S3 creds), and prevent SiYuan from loading the poisoned snippet until cleaned. 3) HUNT: Enumerate every device syncing the same workspace and check for the same conf.json write; pivot to UC #1 (siyuan.exe spawning a shell) on those hosts to see if RCE already fired; confirm all clients are >=3.7.0.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\data\snippets\" and FileName =~ "conf.json"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("siyuan.exe","siyuan-kernel.exe","kernel.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\data\snippets\" and TargetFileName =~ "conf.json"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where not(ActingProcessName has "siyuan")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-54067")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,

// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-54067")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Odido lookalike Okta/SSO phishing-portal domain resolution (ShinyHunters vishing) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] ShinyHunters Okta AiTM: failure-heavy auth flow then success (~10 min) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Rogue Okta MFA factor enrolled as 'Passkey' from Genymobile-emulated Android · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Post-compromise SSO burst: single account rapidly accessing many SaaS apps · [LLM] Bulk SaaS data exfil: high-volume automated downloads (Salesforce/SharePoint/Drive/Slack)
Odido lookalike Okta/SSO phishing-portal domain resolution (ShinyHunters vishing) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts DNS/network connections to attacker-registered lookalike domains that impersonate Odido's SSO, IT-support, or Okta login pages — the AiTM portals ShinyHunters (UNC6661/UNC6671) directs vished employees to. Because the lure arrives by phone/SMS out-of-band, network/DNS telemetry (not corporate email) is the detection surface. Rationale: Applies Huntress-documented ShinyHunters lookalike-domain naming convention (<company>sso[.]com, <company>okta[.]com, <company>support[.]com, <company>internal[.]com, <company>access[.]com) to 'odido'; vishing delivers the link out-of-band so DNS/network egress is the correct pivot rather than EmailEvents. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/threat-library/threat-actors/shinyhunters • https://www.obsidiansecurity.com/blog/behind-the-breach-shinyhunters-2026-voice-phishing-campaign • https://socradar.io/blog/major-cyber-attacks-february-2026/
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1656 T1598.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team sandboxing/analysing the phishing domain (SOC investigation traffic)
  • Brand-monitoring / takedown vendors resolving lookalike domains on the org's behalf
  • Third-party marketing microsite legitimately using an odido- prefixed domain
  • Typo of odido.nl resolving via a parked/registrar landing page
Suppression filter
| where not(RemoteUrl has_any ("odido.nl","odido.com")) and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving host/user and whether a browser process reached the domain; pull the Okta/Entra sign-in for that user in the following 15 min to confirm a session was established. 2) Contain: block the domain at DNS/proxy, force-revoke the user's SSO sessions/tokens and reset credentials + re-enroll MFA. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints for the same domain list, review Okta system log for failure-burst-then-success and new MFA factor enrollment on that account, and check for SSO-burst app access.
let lookalikes = dynamic(["odidosso","odido-sso","myodidosso","odidosupport","odido-support","support-odido","odidookta","odido-okta","odidointernal","odido-internal","odidoaccess","odido-access","odidoazure"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (lookalikes)
| where not(RemoteUrl has_any ("odido.nl","odido.com"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let lookalikes = dynamic(["odidosso","odido-sso","myodidosso","odidosupport","odido-support","support-odido","odidookta","odido-okta","odidointernal","odido-internal","odidoaccess","odido-access","odidoazure"]);
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any (lookalikes)
| where not(DnsQuery has_any ("odido.nl","odido.com"))
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DvcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Odido Lookalike Okta/SSO Phishing Domain Resolution

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationHostname:(*odidosso* OR *odido-sso* OR *myodidosso* OR *odidosupport* OR *odido-support* OR *support-odido* OR *odidookta* OR *odido-okta* OR *odidointernal* OR *odidoaccess* OR *odidoazure*) -@DestinationHostname:(*odido.nl OR *odido.com)

ShinyHunters Okta AiTM: failure-heavy auth flow then success (~10 min) AIExploitation High
Detects the ShinyHunters/UNC6661 adversary-in-the-middle signature in Okta logs: a prolonged, failure-heavy authentication sequence (policy.evaluate_sign_on, app.ad.login.bad_password, core.user.factor.attempt_fail) that ends in a successful session for the same user within a short window — the fingerprint of an operator relaying credentials/MFA through a phishing proxy. Rationale: Uses the exact Okta event names Obsidian documented for this campaign (policy.evaluate_sign_on, app.ad.login.bad_password, core.user.factor.attempt_fail) plus the observed ~10-minute failure-then-success cadence, which distinguishes AiTM relay from a normal fat-finger login. Cross-checked against: • https://www.obsidiansecurity.com/blog/behind-the-breach-shinyhunters-2026-voice-phishing-campaign • https://www.intel471.com/blog/shinyhunters-0-day-attacks-after-patching-find-out-if-you-were-breached
ATT&CKT1621 T1111 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User genuinely forgetting password / fumbling MFA push before succeeding
  • Password rotation day producing repeated app.ad.login.bad_password before cache refresh
  • Flaky mobile network causing multiple factor.attempt_fail before a legit push accept
  • New device onboarding where the user retries several factors
Suppression filter
| where Failures >= 5 and Successes >= 1 and LastSuccess > FirstFail and array_length(SrcIPs) >= 1
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the src IP/ASN and user-agent of the successful session — check for a datacenter/residential-proxy ASN and emulated-Android UA. 2) Contain: revoke all Okta sessions/OAuth tokens for the user, force password reset and MFA re-enrollment, and quarantine any newly enrolled factor. 3) Hunt: check whether a new 'Passkey' MFA device was enrolled right after the success, and whether the account then burst-accessed multiple SSO apps or downloaded bulk SaaS files.
ImAuthentication
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where EventProduct has "Okta"
| summarize Failures = countif(EventResult == "Failure"),
            Successes = countif(EventResult == "Success"),
            FirstFail = minif(TimeGenerated, EventResult == "Failure"),
            LastSuccess = maxif(TimeGenerated, EventResult == "Success"),
            SrcIPs = make_set(SrcIpAddr, 10)
        by TargetUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, 15m)
| where Failures >= 5 and Successes >= 1   // ~10-min failure-heavy AiTM flow ending in success (baseline P99 fail-then-success <=2)
| where LastSuccess > FirstFail
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:okta @outcome.result:FAILURE @evt.name:(policy.evaluate_sign_on OR core.user.factor.attempt_fail OR app.ad.login.bad_password)
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count(eval(Authentication.action="failure")) as failures count(eval(Authentication.action="success")) as successes min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.app="okta" by Authentication.user Authentication.src _time span=15m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where failures >= 5 AND successes >= 1
| eval flowSeconds=lastTime-firstTime
| where flowSeconds <= 900
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count(eval(Authentication.action="failure")) as failures count(eval(Authentication.action="success")) as successes min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.app="okta" by Authentication.user Authentication.src _time span=15m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where failures >= 5 AND successes >= 1
| eval flowSeconds=lastTime-firstTime
| where flowSeconds <= 900
| sort - lastTime
Rogue Okta MFA factor enrolled as 'Passkey' from Genymobile-emulated Android AIInstallation High
Detects ShinyHunters' MFA-persistence step: enrolling an Okta Verify/FastPass factor on an emulated Android device consistently named 'Passkey' with the user-agent com.okta.android.auth/8.19.0 running under Genymobile. This is a high-fidelity, campaign-specific string set rather than generic 'new MFA device' noise. Rationale: Anchored to three corroborated, high-specificity strings from Obsidian/Huntress — the 'Passkey' device name, the Genymobile emulator, and the exact com.okta.android.auth/8.19.0 build — so it fires almost exclusively on this actor's MFA-hijack step. Cross-checked against: • https://www.obsidiansecurity.com/blog/behind-the-breach-shinyhunters-2026-voice-phishing-campaign • https://www.huntress.com/threat-library/threat-actors/shinyhunters
ATT&CKT1556.006 T1098.005
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • QA/security team using a Genymobile emulator to test Okta mobile enrollment
  • Developer legitimately naming a passkey factor 'Passkey' on a physical device (UA will differ)
  • MDM bulk re-enrollment campaign touching user.mfa.factor.update at scale
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the enrollment's src IP/UA and whether it followed a failure-burst login for the same user. 2) Contain: delete the rogue factor, revoke all sessions/tokens, reset credentials and re-enroll MFA on a verified device; disable the account if access spread. 3) Hunt: enumerate all factors enrolled from Genymobile UAs or named 'Passkey' across the tenant, and review SSO-burst / bulk-download activity from the affected accounts.
title: Rogue Okta MFA Enrollment - Passkey Device on Genymobile Emulator (ShinyHunters)
id: 2c7d9a10-5b4e-4f21-8ad3-1e6c9b2f7a44
description: Detects Okta MFA factor enrollment on an emulated Android device named 'Passkey' with the com.okta.android.auth/8.19.0 Genymobile user-agent, matching ShinyHunters (UNC6661/UNC6671) persistence.

Post-compromise SSO burst: single account rapidly accessing many SaaS apps AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the ShinyHunters 'SSO burst' behavior where a hijacked identity enumerates and authenticates into an unusually large number of SSO-connected applications within minutes to locate data repositories. Distinct pivot from the auth-failure UC: this counts distinct downstream apps per account in a tight window. Rationale: Directly implements the 'rapid access to an unusual number of SSO-connected applications' / 'SSO Burst' behavior documented by Obsidian and Intel 471 for this campaign, counting distinct downstream apps per identity per 10-minute bin. Cross-checked against: • https://www.obsidiansecurity.com/blog/behind-the-breach-shinyhunters-2026-voice-phishing-campaign • https://www.intel471.com/blog/shinyhunters-0-day-attacks-after-patching-find-out-if-you-were-breached
ATT&CKT1538 T1528 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Onboarding/offboarding automation or an IdP admin testing app assignments
  • A power user (exec/IT) who legitimately touches many apps at start of day
  • SSO session-refresh storm after a certificate/metadata rotation reissuing tokens for all apps
  • Scripted health-check / synthetic monitoring account probing multiple SaaS apps
Suppression filter
| where AppCount >= 8 and not(AccountDisplayName has_any ("svc-","sync","automation","admin-onboard"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the app list and src IP — flag if apps span unrelated business units (CRM + storage + chat) from one IP/UA. 2) Contain: revoke sessions/tokens, reset credentials, and step-up MFA; temporarily restrict the account to essential apps via conditional access. 3) Hunt: pivot to bulk-download activity in the accessed apps (Salesforce Data Loader, SharePoint/Drive/Slack exports) and to the preceding rogue MFA enrollment.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType has_any ("LoggedIn","Login","Logon","SignIn")
| summarize AppCount = dcount(Application), Apps = make_set(Application, 30), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10)
        by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where AppCount >= 8   // rapid SSO fan-out; typical user P99 <=4 distinct apps / 10m
| order by AppCount desc
ImAuthentication
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where EventProduct has "Okta" and EventResult == "Success"
| summarize AppCount = dcount(TargetAppName), Apps = make_set(TargetAppName, 30), SrcIPs = make_set(SrcIpAddr, 10)
        by ActorUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where AppCount >= 8   // SSO burst threshold; baseline P99 <=4 distinct apps / 10m
| order by AppCount desc
source:okta @evt.name:user.authentication.sso @outcome.result:SUCCESS
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true dc(Authentication.app) as appCount values(Authentication.app) as apps values(Authentication.src) as srcs min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action="success" Authentication.vendor_product="Okta" by Authentication.user _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where appCount >= 8
| sort - appCount
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(Authentication.app) as appCount values(Authentication.app) as apps values(Authentication.src) as srcs min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action="success" Authentication.vendor_product="Okta" by Authentication.user _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where appCount >= 8
| sort - appCount
Bulk SaaS data exfil: high-volume automated downloads (Salesforce/SharePoint/Drive/Slack) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the ShinyHunters exfiltration stage — a hijacked account pulling a very large number of files within a sustained window (Obsidian observed ~90-minute automated download sessions and downloads seconds apart), plus PowerShell-driven SharePoint/OneDrive bulk downloads on the endpoint. Matches the 88GB / 15M-record theft profile from the Odido breach. Rationale: Implements Obsidian's documented exfil signature — high-volume downloads within seconds over a ~90-minute automated session across Google Drive/Slack/SharePoint plus PowerShell SharePoint/OneDrive pulls — matching Odido's disclosed 88GB / 15M-record theft. Cross-checked against: • https://www.obsidiansecurity.com/blog/behind-the-breach-shinyhunters-2026-voice-phishing-campaign • https://socradar.io/blog/major-cyber-attacks-february-2026/
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1530 T1213
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate large migration / eDiscovery / backup export by IT
  • Employee bulk-downloading their own project folder before leaving or for offline work
  • OneDrive/SharePoint sync client doing a full re-sync after cache reset
  • Data-science pipeline account exporting datasets on schedule
Suppression filter
| where Downloads >= 100 and WindowSec <= 5400 and not(AccountDisplayName has_any ("backup","svc-","migration","ediscovery"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the account, src IP/app, and whether downloads span sensitive repositories (CRM/customer-contact data); check if PowerShell UA or Salesforce Data Loader was involved. 2) Contain: revoke sessions/tokens, block the src IP, disable the account, and preserve the download logs for scope. 3) Hunt: correlate back to the rogue MFA enrollment and SSO burst for the same identity, and check for the account leaving internal security Slack channels or extortion email from shinycorp@tutanota.com / shinygroup@onionmail.com.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType has "Download"   // FileDownloaded, FileSyncDownloadedFull, FileDownloadedFromSharePoint
| summarize Downloads = count(), Apps = make_set(Application, 10), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), FirstDl = min(Timestamp), LastDl = max(Timestamp)
        by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, bin(Timestamp, 30m)
| extend WindowSec = datetime_diff('second', LastDl, FirstDl)
| where Downloads >= 100 and WindowSec <= 5400   // >=100 files inside a <=90-min automated pull
| order by Downloads desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where Operation in ("FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull","FileSyncDownloadedPartial")
| summarize Downloads = count(), DistinctFiles = dcount(SourceFileName), FirstDl = min(TimeGenerated), LastDl = max(TimeGenerated)
        by UserId, ClientIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 30m)
| extend WindowSec = datetime_diff('second', LastDl, FirstDl)
| where Downloads >= 100 and WindowSec <= 5400   // >=100 files inside a <=90-min automated pull
| order by Downloads desc
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/(sharepoint\.com|-my\.sharepoint\.com|graph\.microsoft\.com|onedrive)/i
| CommandLine=/(Invoke-WebRequest|iwr|DownloadFile|Start-BitsTransfer|Invoke-RestMethod)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
index=o365 Operation IN ("FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull","FileSyncDownloadedPartial")
| bin _time span=30m
| stats count as downloads dc(SourceFileName) as distinctFiles values(ClientIP) as ips min(_time) as firstDl max(_time) as lastDl by UserId _time
| eval windowSeconds=lastDl-firstDl
| where downloads >= 100 AND windowSeconds <= 5400
| sort - downloads
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

URGENT - Progress Tells ShareFile Customers to Shut Down Storage Zone Controllers Over Security Threat

The Hacker News
2026-07-10 9 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Progress Software has told ShareFile customers to shut down the Windows servers running their Storage Zone Controllers, confirming to The Hacker News that it is responding to a "credible external security threat." The company has temporarily disabled access to the affected accounts, a step it says it took "out of an abundance of caution" while it works with internal and external security

CVEsCVE-2026-2699 CVE-2026-2701 CVE-2023-24489
ATT&CKT1190 T1486 T1555.003
