UNC6395 follow-on AWS API use from Drift-harvested AKIA keys via Tor egress AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects AWS CloudTrail API activity sourced from the UNC6395 IP set — the follow-on stage where AWS access keys (AKIA) harvested out of exfiltrated Salesforce Case/User data are used against victim AWS accounts, frequently over Tor exit nodes. Pivots on a completely different log source (CloudTrail) than the Salesforce-side UCs. Rationale: GTIG confirmed UNC6395 specifically searched exfiltrated Salesforce data for AKIA AWS keys and Snowflake tokens; any CloudTrail call from the 20 campaign IPs (Tor + DigitalOcean/AWS) is a high-fidelity signal of harvested-key use. Uses the exact IOC IP set; Falcon/Sentinel empty because CloudTrail is not FDR endpoint telemetry nor in the provided Sentinel schema. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/data-theft-salesforce-instances-via-salesloft-drift • https://www.ic3.gov/CSA/2025/250912.pdf
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1552.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An engineer legitimately using AWS CLI over Tor or a privacy VPN that egresses a recycled Tor exit node
  • CI/CD or SaaS integration hosted on DigitalOcean (208.68.36.90 range) making sanctioned API calls
  • Tor exit-node IP reassigned to unrelated benign traffic after the Aug 2025 campaign
  • Penetration test / red-team using anonymised egress against the AWS account
  • Third-party managed-service provider operating from cloud egress overlapping a listed IP
Suppression filter
| filter userAgent not like /aws-internal/ and userIdentity.type != "AWSService"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the IAM principal / access key (userIdentity.arn) used from the flagged IP and correlate the AKIA key against any secret found in exfiltrated Salesforce data; check whether the key had prior activity from this IP/region. 2) Contain: immediately deactivate and rotate the implicated access key, apply a deny-all policy or session revocation to the principal, and block the source IPs via SCP/WAF. 3) Hunt: enumerate all actions that key performed (IAM changes, S3 GetObject, CreateUser, persistence), review for new access keys or roles created, and rotate every AWS/Snowflake credential that was stored in Salesforce records.

New MODBEACON RAT Uses gRPC Streaming for Encrypted C2 Traffic

The Hacker News

The China-linked cybercrime group known as Silver Fox has been attributed to a new Rust-based remote access trojan (RAR) called MODBEACON. Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] MODBEACON scheduled-task persistence pointing to user-writable path · Suspicious browser extension installation · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] MODBEACON gRPC/CDN heartbeat beaconing from non-browser user-path process · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
MODBEACON scheduled-task persistence pointing to user-writable path AIInstallation Medium
Hunts MODBEACON's persistence step where the separated loader/beacon registers a scheduled task whose action points to a binary staged in a user-writable path (AppData/Temp/Public/Downloads/ProgramData) after a counterfeit SEO-poisoned installer runs. Article-specific because it pairs schtasks /create with the temp/user staging paths MODBEACON's memory-resident loader drops into, rather than the Program Files paths legitimate installers use. Rationale: Anchors on the article's explicit 'setting persistence using scheduled tasks' plus the memory-resident loader staging in user-writable/temp paths rather than Program Files; no second source corroborated MODBEACON IOCs (search returned only Xray/V2Ray project pages confirming the gRPC transport it reuses exists), so this is behaviour-based and safe to ship without IOCs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/xtls/xray-core
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate software updaters (Google/Edge/Adobe) that stage in ProgramData/AppData and register update tasks
  • Portable apps run from Downloads that self-register a scheduled task
  • IT deployment/RMM tooling creating tasks from a temp staging directory
  • Developer/build tooling scripting schtasks /create from a temp workspace
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("googleupdate.exe","microsoftedgeupdate.exe","officeclicktorun.exe","msiexec.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full schtasks /create command line and the task action path; inspect the parent process (InitiatingProcess) — confirm whether it descends from a recently downloaded installer/ZIP and whether the target binary is signed. 2) Contain: if the action binary is unsigned and in a user-writable path, disable/delete the task (schtasks /delete), isolate the host, and quarantine the referenced binary. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for outbound HTTPS beaconing to Amazon/Cloudflare CDN from non-browser processes and for the originating counterfeit-installer ZIP in Downloads.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Public\", @"\Downloads\", @"\ProgramData\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create"
| where CommandLine has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Public\", @"\Downloads\", @"\ProgramData\")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Scheduled Task Persistence Pointing to User-Writable Path (MODBEACON)
id: 6f2b1c94-0a7d-4d3e-9c2a-8f1e5b3a7c11
description: Detects schtasks.exe creating a scheduled task whose action references a binary in a user-writable path, consistent with MODBEACON loader/beacon persistence.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-modbeacon-rat-uses-grpc-streaming.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/10
tags:
  - attack.t1053.005
  - attack.persistence
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: '/create'
  paths:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '\AppData\'
      - '\Temp\'
      - '\Public\'
      - '\Downloads\'
      - '\ProgramData\'
  condition: selection and paths
level: medium
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*\schtasks.exe OR *\SCHTASKS.EXE OR *\Schtasks.exe) @CommandLine:(*create*) @CommandLine:(*\AppData\* OR *\Temp\* OR *\Public\* OR *\Downloads\* OR *\ProgramData\*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\schtasks\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/\/create/i
| CommandLine=/\\(AppData|Temp|Public|Downloads|ProgramData)\\/i
| table([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName, ParentImageFileName])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe AND Processes.process="*/create*" AND (Processes.process="*\\AppData\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Temp\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Public\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Downloads\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\ProgramData\\*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where user!="*$" | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe AND Processes.process="*/create*" AND (Processes.process="*\\AppData\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Temp\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Public\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Downloads\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\ProgramData\\*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where user!="*$" | sort - lastTime
MODBEACON gRPC/CDN heartbeat beaconing from non-browser user-path process AICommand & Control Low
Hunts MODBEACON's encrypted gRPC-over-HTTP/2 C2 heartbeats fronted by Amazon and Cloudflare CDN, surfacing non-browser processes running from user-writable paths that make sustained, regular outbound HTTPS connections. Article-specific because it targets the memory-resident beacon (payload staged by a counterfeit installer, not an installed app) exhibiting periodic heartbeat cadence to CDN infrastructure rather than normal browsing. Rationale: Targets the article's headline behaviour — encrypted gRPC/HTTP2 heartbeat C2 fronted by Amazon/Cloudflare CDN — by combining the memory-resident beacon's user-writable staging path, a non-browser initiator, and sustained regular-cadence egress; kept as a hunt because no C2 domains/IPs were published (only the QiAnXin-sourced THN article, corroborated only for the Xray/V2Ray gRPC transport it reuses). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/xtls/xray-core
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573.002 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Auto-updaters/telemetry agents staged in ProgramData beaconing to CDN endpoints
  • Electron or portable apps run from Downloads polling a CDN-hosted API
  • EDR/RMM agents in ProgramData with regular check-in cadence to cloud infrastructure
  • Software licensing/heartbeat services legitimately hosted behind CloudFront/Cloudflare
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessSHA256 !in ((DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory | summarize by SHA256="")) or InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sensendr.exe","msmpeng.exe","googleupdate.exe","microsoftedgeupdate.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating binary (hash, path, signer) and check whether it is a known application; review the connection interval regularity and whether the destination is Cloudflare/CloudFront fronting an otherwise unknown domain. 2) Contain: if the binary is unsigned/memory-resident with no install footprint, isolate the host and block the destination IP/domain at the proxy/firewall. 3) Hunt: look for a sibling scheduled-task persistence entry (UC1), host-fingerprinting discovery commands immediately preceding first beacon, and the counterfeit-installer ZIP source in Downloads.
let Browsers = dynamic(["chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","iexplore.exe","opera.exe"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemotePort in (443, 80)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ (Browsers)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Public\", @"\Downloads\")
| extend IsCdn = tostring(RemoteUrl) has_any ("cloudfront.net","amazonaws.com","cloudflare","cdn")
| summarize ConnCount=count(), DistinctMinutes=dcount(bin(Timestamp,1m)), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Remotes=make_set(RemoteUrl,10), AnyCdn=max(IsCdn) by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256, RemoteIP
| where DistinctMinutes >= 20 and ConnCount >= 40
| order by ConnCount desc

| where DistinctMinutes >= 20 and ConnCount >= 40

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationPort:(443 OR 80) @Image:(*\AppData\* OR *\Temp\* OR *\ProgramData\* OR *\Public\* OR *\Downloads\*) -@Image:(*\chrome.exe OR *\msedge.exe OR *\firefox.exe OR *\brave.exe OR *\iexplore.exe OR *\opera.exe)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemotePort=443
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(AppData|Temp|ProgramData|Public|Downloads)\\/i

| tstats `summariesonly` count as ConnCount dc(_time) as DistinctSeconds min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.dest) as dest from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest_port=443 OR All_Traffic.dest_port=80) AND (All_Traffic.process_path="*\\AppData\\*" OR All_Traffic.process_path="*\\Temp\\*" OR All_Traffic.process_path="*\\ProgramData\\*" OR All_Traffic.process_path="*\\Public\\*" OR All_Traffic.process_path="*\\Downloads\\*") AND NOT (All_Traffic.process_name IN (chrome.exe,msedge.exe,firefox.exe,brave.exe,iexplore.exe,opera.exe)) by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.process_name All_Traffic.dest_ip | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where ConnCount>=40 | sort - ConnCount

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0a
status: experimental
description: |
    Registry writes under the browser extension policy keys —
    administrative install of an extension. Often used by adware /
    info-stealers to bypass user-level extension controls.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1176/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1176
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    category: registry_event
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetObject|contains:
            - '\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Group-policy-managed extension whitelists
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
    where (Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\*")
    by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
    where (Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\*")
    by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"

      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

Critical

Unpatched XRING Flaw in XQUIC Lets Remote Clients Crash HTTP/3 Servers

The Hacker News
2026-07-10 8 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A single wrong variable on one line in XQUIC, Alibaba's QUIC and HTTP/3 library, lets any remote client crash the server with a short burst of completely legal traffic. There is no patch. FoxIO researcher Sébastien Féry&nbsp;disclosed the flaw on July 8&nbsp;and nicknamed it XRING. He says it needs no login and no malformed packets: about 260 bytes of ordinary QPACK traffic takes the server

CVEsCVE-2026-42530

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Tengine/XQUIC HTTP/3 worker crash-loop via glibc fortify abort (XRING DoS) · [LLM] Tengine/nginx HTTP/3 worker respawn storm (XRING crash-loop symptom) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Tengine/XQUIC HTTP/3 worker crash-loop via glibc fortify abort (XRING DoS) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts repeated aborts/segfaults of the Tengine or XQUIC-linked HTTP/3 worker process in Linux syslog. The XRING QPACK ring-buffer overflow is caught by glibc _FORTIFY_SOURCE=2, which prints 'buffer overflow detected' and raises SIGABRT (signal 6); repeated occurrences on an HTTP/3 front-end indicate the ~260-byte QPACK DoS being replayed rather than a one-off bug. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete crash mechanism (glibc _FORTIFY_SOURCE=2 -> 'buffer overflow detected'/SIGABRT) plus the named vulnerable software (XQUIC/libxquic, Tengine). The QUIC payload is encrypted on the wire, so the server-side abort signature is the only reliable telemetry; a repeat threshold separates a DoS replay from an incidental crash. No CIM datamodel covers process-crash syslog, so SPL is a raw index search. Cross-checked against: • https://www.penligent.ai/hackinglabs/cve-2026-42530-2/ • https://github.com/alibaba/xquic • https://socprime.com/blog/cve-2026-42530-critical-nginx-http-3-flaw-can-trigger-dos-and-possible-rce/
ATT&CKT1499.004
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Unrelated nginx/Tengine third-party module segfault after an upgrade
  • OOM-killer terminating a worker under memory pressure (SIGKILL, not SIGABRT — usually excluded by message tokens)
  • Disk-full or config-parse abort during deploy
  • A genuine but non-malicious QPACK/HTTP-3 stability bug hit by a real client
  • Fuzzing/pentest activity from an authorized internal scanner
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage !has "Out of memory" and SyslogMessage !has "oom-kill" and SyslogMessage !has "emerg" and SyslogMessage !has "could not open"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full syslog lines on the affected host; confirm the process is the HTTP/3 front-end (Tengine/xquic) and that the crash message is a fortify/SIGABRT overflow, then check whether the site listens on UDP/443 with http3 enabled and QPACK dynamic table on. 2) Contain: apply the vendor workaround — set SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY to 0 (disables the QPACK dynamic table) or disable HTTP/3 on the listener until a fixed XQUIC release ships. 3) Hunt: pivot to firewall/QUIC flow logs for the source IPs sending short (~260-byte) UDP/443 bursts immediately before each crash, and check other Tengine/XQUIC front-ends for the same crash signature.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where ProcessName in~ ("tengine","nginx","xquic") or SyslogMessage has_any ("tengine","nginx","xquic","libxquic")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("buffer overflow detected","stack smashing detected","segfault","signal 6","SIGABRT","general protection")
| summarize CrashCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SampleMsg = any(SyslogMessage) by Computer, ProcessName
| where CrashCount >= 3   // 3+ HTTP/3 worker aborts in 24h = likely XRING replay, not a one-off crash
| order by CrashCount desc
source:linux.syslog (@process.name:(tengine OR nginx) OR *xquic* OR *libxquic*) (*"buffer overflow detected"* OR *"stack smashing detected"* OR *segfault* OR *"signal 6"* OR *SIGABRT*)
APPLICATION
index=os OR index=linux sourcetype IN ("linux_messages_syslog","syslog") (process=tengine OR process=nginx OR "xquic" OR "libxquic") ("buffer overflow detected" OR "stack smashing detected" OR "segfault" OR "signal 6" OR "SIGABRT" OR "general protection")
| stats count as CrashCount min(_time) as firstSeen max(_time) as lastSeen values(_raw) as SampleMsg by host
| where CrashCount>=3
| sort - CrashCount
Tengine/nginx HTTP/3 worker respawn storm (XRING crash-loop symptom) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the process-creation side of the XRING DoS: after each worker aborts, the Tengine/nginx master rapidly forks replacement 'worker process' children. An abnormally high count of worker respawns in a short window on an HTTP/3 front-end indicates the server is being crash-looped, and is visible even when the fortify message format differs or syslog isn't collected. Rationale: Targets the named vulnerable servers (Tengine, nginx) via the 'worker process' command line and a respawn-rate threshold — the observable secondary effect of the XRING abort loop. Distinct pivot from UC1 (process creation vs syslog crash message) so it fires on EDR telemetry even without syslog collection. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/alibaba/xquic • https://socprime.com/blog/cve-2026-42530-critical-nginx-http-3-flaw-can-trigger-dos-and-possible-rce/
ATT&CKT1499.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Planned config reload (SIGHUP) draining and forking workers during a deploy
  • Autoscaling / container restarts spinning up many nginx instances at once
  • Log-rotation reopen triggering worker cycling
  • A high worker_processes count on first boot after a host reboot
  • Legitimate high-traffic reload storms behind a CI/CD pipeline
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "reload" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "-s reload"
Response runbook
1) Triage: on the flagged host, confirm the respawns are unscheduled — check for a concurrent config reload/deploy in change management and correlate with UC1's crash signature in the same window. 2) Contain: if no change window matches, treat as active DoS — apply the SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY=0 workaround or disable HTTP/3 on the listener. 3) Hunt: sweep all internet-facing Tengine/XQUIC hosts for the same respawn pattern and pull QUIC/UDP-443 flow logs for the source IPs driving the short bursts preceding each respawn spike.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(6h)
| where FileName in~ ("nginx","tengine")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "worker process"
| summarize WorkerSpawns = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Host = any(DeviceName) by DeviceId, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where WorkerSpawns >= 10   // steady-state nginx/tengine rarely respawns workers; 10+ in 5m = crash-loop
| order by LastSeen desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(6h)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("nginx","tengine")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "worker process"
| summarize WorkerSpawns = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where WorkerSpawns >= 10
| order by LastSeen desc
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:(nginx OR tengine) @process.command_line:*"worker process"*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/(nginx|tengine)$/i CommandLine=/worker process/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count(as=spawns))
| spawns >= 10
ENDPOINT

| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Internet-facing Zimbra Collaboration exposed to Classic Web Client XSS (10.1.19 / CVE-2025-66376 / CVE-2025-48700)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Zimbra webmail mailbox mass-scrape via burst of /service/soap requests (GhostMail post-XSS collection)
Internet-facing Zimbra Collaboration exposed to Classic Web Client XSS (10.1.19 / CVE-2025-66376 / CVE-2025-48700) AIExploitation High
Surfaces Zimbra Collaboration Suite hosts running a Classic Web Client build below the 10.1.19 fix, and any host still flagged for the two CISA-KEV Zimbra XSS CVEs, prioritising internet-facing systems. Directly operationalises the article's core instruction to patch ZCS 10.1.19, and catches the versionless new flaw by exposing the installed build to the analyst. Rationale: Uses the article's fix version (ZCS 10.1.19) plus the two CISA-KEV Zimbra Classic Web Client XSS CVEs (CVE-2025-66376, CVE-2025-48700) cross-checked against NVD/Tenable and CISA KEV; the inventory build number is what catches the new versionless flaw, and IsInternetFacing prioritises the mass-scale exposure Shadowserver reported. Sentinel lacks the software-inventory table, so its query keys on the two known CVEs + severity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.tenable.com/cve/CVE-2025-66376 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-48700 • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-says-zimbra-flaw-now-exploited-over-10k-servers-vulnerable/ • https://www.securityweek.com/russian-apt-exploits-zimbra-vulnerability-against-ukraine/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host already patched to 10.1.19 but the TVM/scanner snapshot is stale and still reports the old build
  • Non-production Zimbra dev/test instance that is not internet-facing (real exposure but lower priority)
  • A third-party product whose SoftwareName merely contains the string 'zimbra' (connector/plugin), not the ZCS server itself
  • CVE re-scan lag: host remediated CVE-2025-66376 but the vuln feed hasn't refreshed the finding
Suppression filter
| where not (SoftwareVersion has "10.1.19" or SoftwareVersion has "10.1.20")
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit confirm the actual running ZCS build (zmcontrol -v) and whether the Classic Web Client is enabled; treat IsInternetFacing=true hosts as P1. 2) Contain: expedite upgrade to ZCS 10.1.19; where patching lags, restrict Classic UI access via WAF/reverse-proxy allow-list and force session invalidation. 3) Hunt: pivot any confirmed-vulnerable, exposed host into UC2 (SOAP mailbox-scrape) and review Zimbra mailbox.log/audit.log for anomalous session reuse or mass GetMsg/Search activity in the exposure window.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where SoftwareVendor has "zimbra" or SoftwareName has "zimbra"
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities | where CveId in ("CVE-2025-66376","CVE-2025-48700") | summarize KnownExploitedCVEs=make_set(CveId) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| extend PatchedToFix = SoftwareVersion has "10.1.19" or SoftwareVersion has "10.1.20"
| where PatchedToFix == false or array_length(KnownExploitedCVEs) > 0
| project DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP, KnownExploitedCVEs, EndOfSupportStatus
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, SoftwareVersion asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SoftwareVendor has "zimbra" or SoftwareName has "zimbra"
| where CveId in ("CVE-2025-66376","CVE-2025-48700") or VulnerabilitySeverityLevel in ("Critical","High")
| summarize CveList=make_set(CveId), any(SoftwareVersion) by DeviceName, SoftwareName, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel
| order by DeviceName asc

Zimbra webmail mailbox mass-scrape via burst of /service/soap requests (GhostMail post-XSS collection) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a single client IP driving an anomalous burst of POSTs to the Zimbra SOAP endpoint (/service/soap) in a short window, consistent with the injected JavaScript payload scraping up to 90 days of mailbox data after XSS session hijack. Targets the post-exploitation collection step documented for Operation GhostMail rather than the (body-embedded) injection itself. Rationale: Grounded in the GhostMail (CVE-2025-66376) TTP corroborated by Seqrite and BleepingComputer: the XSS payload issues SOAP requests to harvest ~90 days of mailbox data. The Zimbra-specific /service/soap endpoint plus a per-source volumetric threshold isolates automated exfiltration from normal chatty webmail without needing an attacker domain the article never disclosed. Cross-checked against: • https://www.seqrite.com/blog/operation-ghostmail-zimbra-xss-russian-apt-ukraine/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-apt28-military-hackers-exploit-zimbra-flaw-in-ukrainian-govt-attacks/

Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Power user with a very large mailbox running a broad full-text search or client-side re-sync
  • Zimbra or third-party backup/archival tooling (e.g. zmsoap automation, AvePoint) pulling mailboxes over SOAP from a service host
  • Newly onboarded account whose desktop/mobile client performs a full initial sync
  • Migration or eDiscovery job exporting mailboxes via the SOAP API
  • Mobile ActiveSync/IMAP gateway proxying many users through one source IP, inflating per-IP counts
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the authenticated Zimbra account behind the SourceIP/session, and check whether the burst aligns with a known backup/migration window or a legitimate large search; review the client user-agent. 2) Contain: if unexplained, invalidate the account's Zimbra sessions (zmmailbox/admin session purge), force credential + 2FA reset, and block the SourceIP at the proxy. 3) Hunt: confirm whether the host is one of the exposed/vulnerable Zimbra servers from UC1, review mailbox.log for the preceding message-open that rendered the crafted email, and check egress logs for DNS/HTTPS exfiltration to rare external domains from affected user endpoints.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where RequestURL has "/service/soap"
| where DeviceProduct has_any ("Zimbra","nginx","NGINX") or DestinationHostName has "zimbra" or ApplicationProtocol has "http"
| summarize SoapRequests=count(), Methods=make_set(RequestMethod), UrlSample=any(RequestURL), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestClientApplication, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where SoapRequests > 500  // legit interactive webmail sessions rarely exceed ~500 SOAP calls/hr; automated 90-day scrape spikes well beyond
| order by SoapRequests desc
WEB

| tstats summariesonly=true allow_old_summaries=true count values(Web.http_method) as methods from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/service/soap*" by Web.src Web.dest Web.site _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where count > 500 | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false allow_old_summaries=true count values(Web.http_method) as methods from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/service/soap*" by Web.src Web.dest Web.site _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where count > 500 | sort - count

VShell backdoor masquerading as Linux kernel thread [kworker/0:2] AICommand & Control High
Hunts the WP-SHELLSTORM crew's remote-access implant: a userland process that renames itself to the kernel-thread name [kworker/0:2] to blend into the process list, dropped in-memory by the SNOWLIGHT loader (memfd_create). Legitimate kernel worker threads never have a backing on-disk/mem image or a real command line, so a 'kworker' process with a genuine executable path is high-fidelity. Rationale: Uses the article's exact masquerade string '[kworker/0:2]' for the VShell implant; kernel threads never carry a real executable path, so the FolderPath/ImageFileName present + kworker name is a near-zero-FP tell. Corroborated by Sysdig and Trellix write-ups of the SNOWLIGHT→VShell chain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/unc5174-chinese-threat-actor-vshell • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/the-silent-fileless-threat-of-vshell/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/04/chinese-hackers-target-linux-systems.html
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom monitoring/HPC agents that intentionally name worker processes 'kworker-*'
  • Container runtimes spawning short-lived helper procs with kworker-like names
  • Security tooling that itself references 'kworker' in a scan command line
  • Developer scripts grepping for kworker in process names (command line contains the token but is benign)
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/var/tmp/","/run/","/home/","memfd") or FolderPath startswith "/proc/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the true FolderPath/SHA256 of the flagged process; a path in /tmp, /dev/shm, /var/tmp or a memfd:/deleted image confirms masquerade. Check parent process for a SNOWLIGHT-style loader. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture memory before kill (payload is fileless), block egress to unknown remote IPs the process holds. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same SHA256/parent across the fleet, review web-server logs on the host for the exploited plugin CVE that led to code exec, and sweep for down.php webshells.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "kworker" or FileName has "kworker"
| where isnotempty(FolderPath) and FolderPath !startswith "["
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "kworker"
| where isnotempty(ActingProcessName) and ActingProcessName !startswith "["
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Nacos auth bypass via spoofed 'Nacos-Server' User-Agent (CVE-2021-29441) AIDelivery High
Hunts the crew's earlier corporate-Java campaign that skipped Nacos authentication by sending the User-Agent 'Nacos-Server' to config endpoints, then pulled 613 config files (AWS/Alibaba/Oracle keys, DB passwords, Alipay RSA keys). Any HTTP request carrying that exact User-Agent against /nacos/ paths is exploitation, not normal traffic. Rationale: The User-Agent string 'Nacos-Server' is the exact backdoor value CVE-2021-29441 keys on (isEnableUserAgentAuthWhite), scoped to /nacos/ config/admin paths named in the advisory — legitimate clients never send it externally. Cross-checked against GitHub Security Lab GHSL-2020-325 and Tenable's CVE-2021-29441 plugin. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylab.github.com/advisories/GHSL-2020-325_326-nacos/ • https://www.tenable.com/plugins/nessus/154416
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.001
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate intra-cluster Nacos node-to-node sync (real Nacos servers do send this UA — scope to external/untrusted source IPs)
  • Internal blue-team vulnerability scanners testing CVE-2021-29441
  • Nuclei/nessus template runs that replay the Nacos-Server UA
  • Load balancer health checks that were mis-configured to spoof the UA
Suppression filter
| where not (ipv4_is_in_range(SourceIP, "10.0.0.0/8") or ipv4_is_in_range(SourceIP, "172.16.0.0/12") or ipv4_is_in_range(SourceIP, "192.168.0.0/16"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SourceIP is external/untrusted (internal Nacos peer sync legitimately uses this UA); check RequestURL for /cs/configs read or /auth/users add. 2) Contain: rotate EVERY credential stored in the Nacos config (cloud keys, DB passwords, RSA keys) — not just the obvious ones — set nacos.core.auth.enabled=true and upgrade to >=1.4.1/2.2.1. 3) Hunt: review outbound connections from the Nacos host, look for follow-on config exfil and any pivot into cloud accounts using the leaked keys.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where RequestClientApplication == "Nacos-Server"
| where RequestURL has "/nacos/"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WEB

WordPress/Joomla webshell (down.php / BestShell) written by web-server account AIInstallation High
Hunts the plant step of WP-SHELLSTORM: the exploited plugin (Breeze CVE-2026-3844, Joomla JCE CVE-2026-48907, etc.) causes the web-server user to write a PHP webshell — the crew's primary backdoor is named down.php, a 4-layer-obfuscated BestShell derivative. A .php file created inside web root by www-data/apache/nginx/php-fpm is the signature of a webshell drop. Rationale: Anchors on the article's named backdoor 'down.php' plus the generic 'web-server user writes .php into web root' shape; the web-server account writing new PHP is rarely legitimate outside of plugin/theme updates. The exact filename branch is alerting-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/exposed-hacker-server-reveals-wp.html
ATT&CKT1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WordPress/Joomla plugin or theme auto-updates writing PHP files
  • WP-CLI or composer deployments run as the web-server user
  • Caching plugins (including Breeze itself) generating .php cache files
  • CMS core updates unpacking new .php files into web root
  • Developer staging deployments run under the apache/nginx account
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("wp-cli","composer","apt","yum","dpkg") or FolderPath has_any ("/cache/","/wp-content/cache/","/tmp/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the flagged file — 4-layer obfuscation / eval/gzinflate/base64 chains or BestShell markers confirm webshell; check FolderPath is inside web root. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, take a copy for IR, pull access logs for the URL of the shell and block the source IPs; patch the exploited plugin (Breeze 2.4.5, JCE 2.9.99.5). 3) Hunt: search for the web-server process spawning /bin/sh (command execution via the shell), and for a VShell [kworker] implant indicating deeper access.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName =~ "down.php" or (FileName endswith ".php" and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("www-data","apache","nginx","httpd","http","daemon","php-fpm"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("php","php-fpm","apache2","httpd","nginx")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName =~ "down.php" or (TargetFileExtension =~ "php" and ActorUsername in~ ("www-data","apache","nginx","httpd","http","daemon"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/down\.php$/i

Web-server process spawning shell/recon binaries (webshell command execution) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts hands-on-keyboard use of the down.php webshell: php-fpm/apache/nginx spawning a shell or recon utility (sh, id, whoami, uname, curl, wget). The BestShell-derived backdoor runs commands, opens reverse shells, and checks which security software is present — all of which surface as a web-server parent spawning a non-PHP child. Rationale: Targets the article's description of down.php running commands / opening reverse shells / enumerating security software — expressed as the web-server parent → shell/recon child process tree, a pivot distinct from the file-write UC. Behaviourally scoped so it is not the generic 'Office spawns script' pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/exposed-hacker-server-reveals-wp.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • PHP apps that legitimately shell out (image processing via ImageMagick convert, PDF generation, git/composer hooks)
  • Monitoring plugins invoking uname/id for host info
  • Backup scripts triggered by the web app calling curl/wget
  • CI deploy hooks run under the web-server user
  • Health-check endpoints that exec whoami/uname
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("convert","gs ","ghostscript","composer","git ","/backup/") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: read ProcessCommandLine of the child — recon (id;uname;whoami), a reverse shell (bash -i, nc -e), or a download (curl/wget to an unknown IP) confirms webshell use; identify the parent PHP file. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process chain, block the remote IP, and quarantine the identified webshell (likely down.php). 3) Hunt: pivot to DeviceFileEvents for the webshell write, look for a VShell [kworker] implant on the same host, and review whether cloud/DB credentials on the host were accessed.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("php-fpm","php","apache2","httpd","nginx")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","id","whoami","uname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","php","apache2","httpd","nginx")
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","id","whoami","uname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Web Server Process Spawning Shell or Recon Binary
id: d47b8c62-9e1a-4f35-a6c0-2b8f1d5e7a09
description: Detects a web-server process (php-fpm/apache/nginx) spawning a shell or recon utility, indicating webshell command execution (WP-SHELLSTORM down.php).
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering

logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/php-fpm'
      - '/php'
      - '/apache2'
      - '/httpd'
      - '/nginx'
    Image|endswith:
      - '/sh'
      - '/bash'
      - '/dash'
      - '/id'
      - '/whoami'
      - '/uname'
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'

level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:(sh OR bash OR dash OR id OR whoami OR uname OR curl OR wget OR nc OR ncat) @process.parent.name:(php-fpm OR php OR apache2 OR httpd OR nginx)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(php-fpm|php|apache2|httpd|nginx)/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(sh|bash|dash|zsh|id|whoami|uname|curl|wget|nc|ncat|python3?|perl)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name IN ("php-fpm","php","apache2","httpd","nginx") AND Endpoint.Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","id","whoami","uname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl") by Endpoint.Processes.dest Endpoint.Processes.user Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name Endpoint.Processes.process_name Endpoint.Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint.Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name IN ("php-fpm","php","apache2","httpd","nginx") AND Endpoint.Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","id","whoami","uname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl") by Endpoint.Processes.dest Endpoint.Processes.user Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name Endpoint.Processes.process_name Endpoint.Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint.Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents

          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'

            - '-ep bypass'

    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

Critical

Study of 281 Free Android VPN Apps Finds Traffic Leaks, Unencrypted Data, and Tracking

The Hacker News
2026-07-10 6 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Researchers ran 281 of the most popular free VPN apps on the Google Play Store through a new testing system and found that many fail at the basics people install a VPN for, i.e., keeping their traffic private and secure. The apps flagged with at least one problem have been installed more than 2.4 billion times. The problems are basic, not sophisticated. 29 apps let user traffic leak outside

CVEsCVE-2016-6329 CVE-2016-2183
ATT&CKT1190 T1486 T1555.003

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.

| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access

    category: file_access
    product: windows

    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

            - '\Cookies'

level: high

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2016-6329", "CVE-2016-2183")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2016-6329", "CVE-2016-2183")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents

Hackers Use Fake Microsoft Entra Passkey Enrollment to Gain Microsoft 365 Access

The Hacker News
2026-07-10 12 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A threat actor has been targeting organizations spanning multiple sectors with voice-based fake security requests that prompt Microsoft 365 users to enroll a new Entra passkey with an aim to carry out data extortion attacks. The threat actor, tracked by Okta under the moniker O-UNC-066, has deployed a panel-controlled phishing kit that's capable of targeting the passkey enrollment process. The

ATT&CKT1190 T1486 T1555.003 T1566
Domainsassignpasskey.com deploypasskey.com passkeydeploy.com passkeyadd.com setpasskey.com

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] O-UNC-066 passkey-themed vishing phishing domain contact (assignpasskey/deploypasskey/etc.) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] O-UNC-066 passkey phishing-kit URL-path fingerprint (/backend.php, /submit-authenticator, /passkey/check) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Rogue Entra passkey/FIDO2 registration from O-UNC-066 operator ASN (DDoS-Guard/IQWeb) · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
O-UNC-066 passkey-themed vishing phishing domain contact (assignpasskey/deploypasskey/etc.) AIDelivery High
Hunts endpoint/DNS resolution or connection to the five O-UNC-066 ('Pink') passkey-themed phishing domains used to lure Microsoft 365 users mid-vishing call into enrolling an attacker passkey. Article-specific because it pins the exact registered domain set rather than a generic phishing pattern. Rationale: Uses the five exact registered domains from the article's IOC block, all confirmed in Okta's primary write-up. Any resolution is a strong pre-compromise vishing signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.okta.com/blog/threat-intelligence/vishing-actors-target-microsoft-entra-passkey-enrollment-/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/entra-passkey-enrollment-vishing-targets-microsoft-365-users/
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security-awareness team detonating the phishing domains in a sandbox/test range
  • Threat-intel analyst manually browsing the IOC domains during triage
  • URL-scanning/sandbox appliances auto-resolving reported domains
  • Corporate DNS sinkhole/RPZ probe traffic against known-bad lists
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user/host that resolved the domain and check whether it followed an inbound phone call or unusual sign-in; pull recent Entra sign-ins for that UPN. 2) Contain: force sign-out + revoke refresh tokens for the user, reset password, and quarantine any attacker-registered auth method (see UC2). 3) Hunt: sweep DNS/proxy org-wide for all five domains and any *passkey* subdomains over 30d; cross-reference against Entra 'User registered security info' events in the same window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("assignpasskey.com","deploypasskey.com","passkeydeploy.com","passkeyadd.com","setpasskey.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let PasskeyDomains = dynamic(["assignpasskey.com","deploypasskey.com","passkeydeploy.com","passkeyadd.com","setpasskey.com"]);
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Name has_any (PasskeyDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, IPAddresses = Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc
